Which inline highlighting is easiest to read?

Eight prototypes, identical input and line correspondence. Stronger blue marks the changed text inside a pale blue changed region. This is a standalone rendering using Bygone’s colors, not a shipped application change.

52designed cases
441real repository line pairs
12,000fuzz algorithm runs
See resultsexisting regression suite × 8 engines

A bracket oracle is an explicitly chosen readability target, not objective semantic truth. Unicode warnings identify highlights that cut through a displayed character. Most variants can inherit unsafe boundaries from the initial word tokenizer. The bounded and identifier-parts variants repair those boundaries.

Fewer highlighted characters or matching islands is not automatically better. The corpus is the current engine’s corresponding changed lines (≤500 characters) from the last 40 source commits; this is a single-project sample. Timing is a local microbenchmark and excludes rendering. Character algorithms here use graphemes; this is not a reproduction of Meld’s matcher. Existing whitespace handling and inline length limits stay intact in engine tests.

Validation and remaining limitations

The preferred prototype is Identifier parts + edges: word anchors, camelCase/acronym/underscore parts, then identical-edge trimming. Unicode boundary repair and a work limit are included. This is a conservative experimental recommendation, not a measured human-readability winner.

Both unrestricted character variants fail the same two tests: they split the replaced word “instrument” instead of emphasizing it wholly. Other variants pass after normalizing adjacent highlighted fragments. All seven alternatives preserve alignment, blocks, reflows and text reconstruction in 202 integration cases each.

Stress tests include 500, 2,000 and 9,990-character strings: unrelated text, local edits, and repeated camel-case components. Some unbounded character variants exceed the 2.5-second subprocess limit. Identifier parts + edges completes every stress case, using edge-only fallback for large replacement spans. Raw data: stress.json.

Only this repository was sampled. Designed targets are subjective; no user reading-speed study, direct Meld implementation comparison, full application test suite, or desktop rendering verification was performed. Browser inspection uses this standalone comparison. No production source was changed by this experiment.

Methods and reproducibility

Run node run.cjs, node stress.cjs, and node report.cjs from this directory. Source snapshot, corpus patches, structured results, and individual regression logs are included. Recorded commit: c08545c9976f53c5d8632ddbaf0645fde3ba41cb. Rerunning resamples the current source and history. Source SHA256: 161aea6b5a72b48e3b9c221ff3874a19f0ef1b8c60ea275a74665f3f8f39a361. Node v26.10.0, diff 5.2.2.

Smart baseline discards internal matching islands shorter than 3 graphemes and requires 50% retained graphemes per changed word span. The threshold sweep varies these to 2–4 and 35–65%. These are experimental policies, not tuned production defaults.

Anchored refinement preserves identical prefixes and suffixes before matching the middle, then absorbs internal matches shorter than 3 graphemes. The bounded variant also falls back to edge trimming for large spans and repairs inherited Unicode boundaries.

The identifier-parts variant adds camelCase, acronym, and underscore boundaries within word replacements, matches whole parts, then trims matching edges. It uses no character-similarity score or minimum-match-length setting. Replacement spans with a length product above 250,000 fall back to edge trimming; this is a computational budget, not a similarity judgment.

Invariants check source reconstruction, presence/absence of changes, grapheme boundaries, and reversal stability. Boundary and symmetry issues are measured, not suppressed. Integration checks preserve rows, blocks, reflow anchors, quality, and segment reconstruction across all candidates.
